title: Monolith vs Modular Monolith vs Microservices
description: Understand the architectural spectrum from monolith to microservices, and learn to choose the right structure for your team size, domain clarity, and scale requirements.

data.text: Architecture is not a binary choice between monolith and microservices. It is a spectrum. At one end is the classic monolith: a single deployable unit with no enforced internal boundaries. At the other is microservices: many small, independently deployable services communicating over a network. In the middle is the modular monolith: a single deployable unit with strict internal boundaries, each module owning its data and exposing a public interface. The senior engineer picks the point on this spectrum that matches the team's size, the domain's clarity, and the system's scale.

In a C# solution, all three architectures are feasible. A classic monolith is a single ASP.NET Core project. A modular monolith is a solution with multiple class library projects that enforce boundaries through access modifiers and dependency rules. Microservices are multiple ASP.NET Core projects deployed independently. The transition between these states is smoother than most engineers realize: a well-structured modular monolith can become microservices with relatively modest refactoring because the boundaries were already enforced.

cards.title: Classic Monolith
cards.description: A single deployable unit with no enforced internal boundaries.
pros: Simplest to develop, test, and deploy
No network overhead or distributed complexity
Strong data consistency through a single database
Easiest to refactor across module boundaries
cons: No enforced boundaries; any code can reach any other code
Long compile and deployment times as the codebase grows
Difficult for large teams to work without stepping on each other

cards.title: Modular Monolith
cards.description: A single deployable unit with strict internal boundaries between modules.
pros: Strong data consistency and simple deployment
Easier to extract into microservices later
cons: Module interface design can be challenging

cards.title: Microservices
cards.description: Multiple small, independently deployable services with their own data stores.
pros: Fault isolation: one service failure does not bring down the system
cons: Debugging across service boundaries is difficult

data.title: Architecture selection criteria
items: Start with a monolith if the team has fewer than five engineers or the domain is unclear.
Evolve to a modular monolith when the codebase grows beyond what a single team can maintain safely.
Evolve to microservices only when you have clear domain boundaries, multiple autonomous teams, and a genuine need for independent scaling.
Never skip the modular monolith stage. Extracting microservices from a classic monolith is much harder than extracting from a modular monolith.

data.title: The evolutionary path
data.text: Most successful systems follow this path: monolith, then modular monolith, then microservices. This is not because microservices are the ultimate goal; it is because each stage is the simplest architecture that solves the current problem. The modular monolith is not a compromise; it is the right architecture for the middle phase of most systems' lives.

A modular monolith in C# is implemented as a solution with multiple projects. Each project represents a module and has strict rules about what it can reference. The API project is the composition root that wires everything together.

data.title: Solution structure for a modular monolith
data.content: A typical .NET solution structure that enforces module boundaries through project references.
data.code:
MyApp.sln
  src/
    MyApp.Api/           <-- Composition root, references all modules
      Program.cs
      Extensions/        <-- DI registration, middleware
    MyApp.Orders/        <-- Orders module
      Domain/            <-- Entities, value objects
      Application/       <-- Use cases, interfaces
      Infrastructure/    <-- EF Core DbContext, repositories
    MyApp.Inventory/     <-- Inventory module
      Domain/
      Application/
      Infrastructure/
    MyApp.Payments/      <-- Payments module
      Domain/
      Application/
      Infrastructure/
    MyApp.SharedKernel/  <-- Shared types only (no business logic)
      Events/
      Results/
  tests/
    MyApp.Orders.Tests/
    MyApp.Inventory.Tests/
    MyApp.Payments.Tests/

data.text: Module boundaries are enforced through project references and access modifiers. The Orders module cannot reference the Payments module directly; it can only reference the shared kernel and its own internals. Communication between modules happens through MediatR notifications or domain events, which are defined in the shared kernel.

data.title: Module communication with domain events
data.content: Using MediatR to communicate between modules without direct references.

data.text: Extract a module into a microservice when it has a clear domain boundary, needs independent scaling, requires a different technology stack, or is owned by a different team. Do not extract prematurely. A module that changes frequently is actually better kept in the monolith, because refactoring across service boundaries is much slower than refactoring within a single codebase.

data.title: Map your project to the architecture spectrum
data.description: Evaluate your current project and determine where it falls on the monolith spectrum.
steps: Describe your current architecture in one sentence.
Identify the internal boundaries in your codebase: do they exist, and are they enforced?
Count the number of engineers working on the codebase.
Identify any modules that would benefit from independent scaling or deployment.
Determine the current stage: monolith, modular monolith, or microservices.
If you are a monolith, design one module boundary. If you are microservices, identify one service that could be merged back into a monolith for simplicity.
data.expectedOutcome: A self-assessment of your project's architecture with one concrete improvement recommendation.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Architecture is a spectrum: monolith, modular monolith, microservices.
Start simple and evolve only when the current architecture no longer solves the problem.
The modular monolith is the sweet spot for most medium-sized teams and domains.
Enforce module boundaries through project structure and access modifiers, not just conventions.
data.takeaway: Senior engineers do not pick an architecture because it is popular; they pick the simplest architecture that solves the team's actual problems at the current scale.
